newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Heavy fighting around Goma, east Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Heavy fighting around Goma, east Zaire.

text.p: Heavy fighting erupted around the eastern Zairean town of Goma on Thursday between rebels and their Hutu foes holed up in the teeming refugee camp of Mugunga.
Mortar, anti-aircraft and heavy machinegun fire rocked the area around the camp about 10 km (six miles) west of the town on Rwanda's border.

Journalists were kept away from the front line but the fighting appeared to be directly linked to the planned deployment in the area of a Canadian-led multinational force, diplomatic and other sources said.
Most of the fire appeared to come from the rebel side with controlled and occasional volleys from multi-barrelled rocket launchers on strategic Mount Goma overlooking the area.

But mortar rounds came out of the sprawling camp -- five km (three miles) across -- where thousands of fighters mingle among a huge concentration of Hutu refugees. The fighting eased after several hours.
Some 800 displaced Zaireans reached Goma by boat on Thursday and many reported cholera and heavy battles between rebel and Hutu forces to the west.
For the second day running rebel anti-aircraft batteries opened up on a light plane circling over Goma, missing it.
The rebels encircle Hutu fighters who in turn guard a perimeter around Mugunga, according to sketchy reports.

The fighting erupted as news broke in Goma that Canada and the United States, key members of the multinational force being prepared to intervene in eastern Zaire, will not disarm the Hutu fighters when they bring aid to the 1.2 million refugees displaced by a month-long rebellion.
Some estimates say Mugunga is now home to 400,000 Hutu refugees, or one third of the Rwandan and Burundian Hutus scattered in eastern Zaire by a month-long rebellion.

The number of fighters is also a mystery. But when the Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 after the genocide against minority Tutsis they included about 40,000 former troops, the FAR, and about 10,000 Interahamwe militiamen.
Some Goma residents said they believed the rebels were trying to take on the Hutu fighters before the arrival of the multinational force in a few days.
"The rebels know they've got a few days to do the job before the force comes in. They're doing it while they've got the chance," one Goma resident told Reuters.
The rebels and the Tutsi-dominated armies of Rwanda and Burundi fear that after the foreign force arrives the Hutus will in effect be protected and able to sit tight, refusing all appeals to go home.
"Obviously the Rwandans will be very disappointed by the mandate for this Canadian-led group," one senior diplomat in the region told Reuters on Thursday.
A senior Rwandan official confirmed that disappointment.

"This is a false start. As long as the international force is not prepared to disarm the ex-FAR and the Interahamwe its objectives will not be achieved," Seth Kamanzi, a presidential adviser, said by telephone from Kigali.
Attention is focused on the Hutu refugees but hundreds of thousands of local Zaireans are also victims of the fighting in the east between an array of forces.

The 800 Zaireans who arrived in rebel-held Goma by boats across Lake Kivu had left Goma by land as rebel forces closed in two weeks ago. They headed through Mugunga to Sake, six km (four miles) west of the camp.
"We left Sake because there is a lot of fighting between Zairean rebels, the Interahamwe and the Mai-Mai (a Zairean tribal militia)," said Lolonga Osakamu, 28.
"We tried to return to Goma via Mugunga but we were blocked on the road by the Interahamwe. The Interahamwe have extended their line outwards from Mugunga to the village of Ndosho.
"They are heavily armed. They have blocked the road and I saw them making defensive positions. We returned to Sake but there is illness in Sake and many people have cholera," he added.
"I only arrived here now with my very small brother," said Kamat Kakul.
"There were 18 members of my family in Sake. We are the only two left. All the others are dead or lost. Three of them died because they were ill. Some were shot and the rest fled," he said.
